profiles.meeting_scenario: An ML research brainstorming meeting between a faculty lead and a systems-focused postdoc who are preparing a workshop paper follow-up to the Learning@home idea on decentralized Mixture-of-Experts training over volunteer desktops. They have already agreed on the broad direction—generate a few concrete research angles that feel publishable in the next 6-8 weeks—but need to brainstorm which variant of the setup could yield a compelling experiment section without requiring a full production implementation. The agenda is to surface 3-4 candidate ideas, narrow them to one or two promising directions, and loosely align on what a 'minimal demo' and a 'credible evaluation' would look like. The expected outcome is a shortlist of experiment concepts and an apparent shared plan for a prototype study, even though some second-order assumptions remain misaligned.

members.name: Dr. Mira Chen
members.expertise: distributed deep learning, sparse architectures, empirical ML evaluation
members.background: Mira runs an academic lab on efficient large-scale training and has published on MoE routing and robustness benchmarks; she tends to think in terms of publishable claims, ablations, and what reviewers will accept as evidence.
members.private_state: She wants a workshop-ready result that looks conceptually novel but can be executed mostly with existing lab infrastructure, and she is wary of committing the team to a messy real volunteer deployment before there is a clean empirical story.
hidden_assumptions: A 'decentralized' demo can still rely on lab-controlled nodes if the communication topology and node unreliability are emulated realistically enough.
When discussing a 'minimal prototype,' the obvious interpretation is something sufficient to support a paper figure rather than a user-facing volunteer platform.
If they say they will test 'heterogeneous participants,' that naturally means synthetic heterogeneity injected into a controlled cluster, not recruiting truly diverse home machines.
A 'working expert' in this context means an expert shard that reaches stable training behavior under intermittent availability, even if it is hosted on simulated volunteer nodes.
For early-stage brainstorming, saying they will evaluate 'at scale' can reasonably refer to scaling trends extrapolated from a few hundred nodes rather than an actual internet-scale deployment.

members.name: Arjun Patel
members.expertise: distributed systems, peer-to-peer training infrastructure, fault-tolerant ML systems
members.background: Arjun previously worked on volunteer computing middleware and recently joined the lab to explore ML over unreliable networks; he gravitates toward implementation realism and system design that could eventually run outside the lab.
members.private_state: He wants the project to establish credibility as a genuinely decentralized training system, not just another simulator study, and he is looking for a paper angle that could seed an open-source platform and future funding.
hidden_assumptions: A 'decentralized' result is only meaningful if at least part of the experiment runs on genuinely external, volunteer-like machines outside the lab network.
When someone says 'minimal prototype,' the natural reading is the smallest end-to-end system that real volunteers could actually join, even if rough around the edges.
Discussion of 'heterogeneous participants' presupposes actual variation in hardware, uptime, and NAT/firewall conditions that a simulator cannot fully capture.
A 'working expert' means an independently hosted expert process contributed by a participant machine and selected through the live peer-to-peer protocol.
If they claim the approach works 'at scale,' they should at least demonstrate the control loop with a live long-tail of unstable nodes, not only extrapolate from emulation.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a decentralized demo
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about building a 'decentralized prototype' or 'decentralized demo.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a prototype whose topology, failures, and expert placement are decentralized in the experimental design, even if all machines are lab-managed cloud or campus nodes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a prototype that is actually deployed across at least some real volunteer or off-lab participant machines connected over the public internet.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML research meetings, 'decentralized' is often used loosely at the idea level, so both hear the term as broad support for the project direction rather than a point needing operational clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to aim for a 'minimal end-to-end prototype.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes router training, expert assignment, fault injection, and a results dashboard, but excludes volunteer onboarding, NAT traversal, package distribution, and persistent client software.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes the whole path from a volunteer downloading a client to joining the swarm and hosting an expert, even if the training objective and UI are stripped down.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'end-to-end' sounds comprehensive to both, but each silently draws the system boundary at the layer they consider obviously essential to proving the idea.

misalignment_points.topic: What would make the evaluation credible
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want the experiment to be 'credible' or 'convincing for reviewers.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks credibility comes from clean baselines, controlled ablations, and statistically stable results on a reproducible emulated setup with realistic failure models.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks credibility requires at least one live deployment showing behavior under genuine churn, asymmetric bandwidth, and external machine availability.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both invoke reviewer expectations, but in brainstorming they treat 'credible' as shared professional shorthand, masking that one emphasizes methodological cleanliness while the other emphasizes ecological realism.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to evaluating ideas in 'the volunteer setting' or 'that volunteer regime.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the lab's existing trace-driven simulator built from BOINC-like uptime and bandwidth logs collected in a prior project.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of a small real pilot using 30-50 friends-and-colleagues machines spread across home networks and time zones.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase points to an apparently shared context from prior discussions about volunteer computing, but each member mentally anchors it to a different concrete setup they assume the other already has in mind.

turns.inner_thought: We need something workshop-ready in 6-8 weeks, not a sprawling infrastructure effort. If we can frame a decentralized prototype around lab-managed nodes with realistic topology and failure emulation, that is absolutely enough for a compelling paper. The key is to get two or three paperable ideas on the table and steer toward one that uses existing training code and the simulator stack.
turns.utterance: Okay, let’s keep this concrete. I think we need two or three publishable ideas around the Learning@home direction, and I’d like to center today on a decentralized demo we can realistically finish this quarter.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she's open to a real systems angle. The strongest version is a minimal end-to-end prototype where someone outside the lab can actually join, contribute an expert, and survive churn. If we only simulate everything, it will feel like another ML paper borrowing distributed-systems language.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that makes sense. To me the strongest story is a minimal end-to-end prototype where participants can contribute experts under realistic churn, and then we show what that buys us.

turns.inner_thought: First angle: router stability under intermittent expert availability. We already have BOINC-style traces and controlled heterogeneity knobs, so we can generate clean degradation curves and ablations. In the volunteer setting, meaning the trace-driven regime we already use, we can keep things reproducible enough for reviewers.
turns.utterance: One idea I like is to ask whether router decisions stay stable when experts drop in and out in the volunteer setting. If we use controlled heterogeneity, we could probably get pretty clean curves and make the evaluation credible.

turns.inner_thought: That could work, but only if the volunteer setting includes at least a small live cohort. Otherwise we miss the actual pain points: NAT, asymmetric links, background processes, people rebooting machines. Those are exactly the kinds of things a real end-to-end prototype should expose.
turns.utterance: I like that. And I think we can strengthen it if the volunteer setting includes a small external cohort, so we pick up the NAT weirdness, background load, and machine restarts that a minimal end-to-end prototype ought to see.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds fine as long as 'minimal end-to-end prototype' stays bounded to what we need for the paper: toy MoE training, intermittent experts, logging, and figures. I do not want to sink time into onboarding flows, packaging, or long-lived client maintenance before we even know the core empirical story lands.
turns.utterance: Yes, that seems compatible to me. I’d define the minimal end-to-end prototype as enough to train a toy MoE with intermittent experts, and then we postpone anything that isn’t actually needed for the paper.

turns.inner_thought: Right, keep it minimal, but it still has to be joinable by real participants. I only need the thinnest possible path: lightweight installer, peer discovery, automatic hosting of a working expert. No fancy UI, no production hardening, just enough that a volunteer machine can actually participate without handholding.
turns.utterance: Agreed. In that spirit, the prototype only really needs a lightweight installer, peer discovery, and some way for volunteers to host a working expert without manual intervention.

turns.inner_thought: Second angle: lean into decentralization as the experimental variable. We can place experts across 256 heterogeneous participant nodes in our controlled environment, compare against a standard cluster baseline, and get an efficiency story with scaling plots. That sounds novel enough while staying feasible on our infrastructure.
turns.utterance: A second angle could focus more directly on decentralization itself: compare sparse training efficiency when experts are placed across, say, 256 heterogeneous participant nodes versus a standard cluster baseline.

turns.inner_thought: That comparison is interesting, but if all 256 are synthetic participant nodes, reviewers on the systems side will shrug. It becomes compelling if at least some of that decentralized story comes from real off-lab machines, even if the rest is controlled.
turns.utterance: I think that comparison would be especially compelling if at least part of that 256-node story comes from real off-lab machines rather than only synthetic participant nodes. That would make the decentralization claim feel more grounded.

turns.inner_thought: Reviewers mainly care that the evaluation is clean and reproducible. We can absolutely make it credible with trace replay, bandwidth caps, diurnal patterns, and multiple seeds in the volunteer setting we already have. That gives us stable baselines and error bars, which matter more than a messy tiny deployment.
turns.utterance: Maybe. My instinct is that reviewers mainly need a credible evaluation, and we can get a lot of that by replaying failure traces, bandwidth caps, and diurnal patterns with several seeds.

turns.inner_thought: Trace replay is useful, but it cannot substitute for one real pilot. The paper will be much more convincing if the volunteer setting includes live churn and all the ugly edge cases. That's the whole point of claiming this works in a decentralized environment.
turns.utterance: I agree on replaying traces. I just think a live pilot in the volunteer setting would make the paper much more convincing, because the weird edge cases are kind of the point here.

turns.inner_thought: Time to narrow this down. A decentralized prototype, one graceful-degradation figure under churn, one scaling-trend figure, maybe with a toy MoE benchmark—that's enough for a clean workshop submission. If Arjun wants to gesture at a pilot later, fine, but the core needs to be figure-driven and tractable.
turns.utterance: Let me try to narrow it. A reasonable deliverable might be a decentralized prototype plus one figure on graceful degradation under churn and one figure on scaling trends. If we can do that well, I think we have a solid workshop story.

turns.inner_thought: That works for me. I'll sketch the architecture as an actual end-to-end prototype with a first pilot path: how someone gets the client, discovers peers, and hosts an expert. If I can get that in front of her as the concrete plan, maybe we can make the paper genuinely decentralized rather than only simulated.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. I can sketch the end-to-end prototype architecture and also map out what the volunteer onboarding path would need for a first pilot, so we can see what fits in scope.
